item.title: Mesa School Bags ₹110 Cr To Launch New On-Campus Courses
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Bengaluru-based Mesa School of Business has raised ₹110 Cr ($11.4 Mn) in its Series A funding round in a mix…
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based Mesa School of Business has raised ₹110 Cr ($11.4 Mn) in its Series A funding round in a mix of debt and equity. The round pegged the business school at a post-money valuation of ₹385 Cr ($40 Mn), cofounder Ankit Agarwal told Inc42.

While the ₹85 Cr equity round was co-led by Dharana Capital and existing backer Elevation Capital, the remaining ₹25 Cr was raised via venture debt from InnoVen Capital and Alteria Capital.

Mesa plans to utilise the fresh capital to strengthen its leadership team, integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into its programmes, deepen partnerships with startups and launch new courses. 

Founded in 2023 by Agarwal and Varun Limaye, Mesa offers on-campus educational programmes for individuals. It currently offers three full-time programmes targeting early-career professionals, fresh graduates and undergraduate students. 

While the startup charges ₹25.4 Lakh in tuition fees for its one-year post-graduate programme, its one-year Forge programme for fresh graduates has a starting fees of ₹15.4 Lakh. The undergraduate programme costs ₹48 Lakh over four years. 

Training Talent For Startups 

Despite being one of India’s fastest-growing employment segments, the local startup ecosystem continues to face a talent gap. Speaking with Inc42, Agarwal said that the talent paucity is especially acute in non-technical roles, which account for nearly 80% of jobs in the sector.

While graduates from premier institutions often have established recruitment pathways into startups, students without access to such networks, Agarwal said, lack a structured route to enter the startup ecosystem.

“If you want to go and work in a startup, there is no one place which sort of builds the right network,” he said.

Unlike conventional business schools, Mesa does not employ full-time faculty, relying instead on startup founders, executives and industry experts to design and deliver its curriculum. Around 2,000 industry professionals have interacted with our students in some capacity, Agarwal said.

“The institutions just don’t have the capability or the incentives to keep changing their curriculum and to keep it super agile over time, and that’s where we felt that we should come in and create talent for the startup ecosystem across levels and functions,” Agarwal said.

On the business front, Mesa’s revenue comes primarily from programme fees, which it collects annually and largely in advance. The experienced-professional postgraduate programme contributes around 40% of revenue, while the undergraduate programme accounts for 35-40%. The fresh-graduate programme contributes around 20%, according to Agarwal.

While the startup is yet to achieve profitability, founder Agarwal claims that most of Mesa’s programmes are approaching operational breakeven. Mesa claims to have grown its business around 2.5X annually over the past two years, Agarwal said, projecting that it will continue to grow at a similar pace in upcoming years. 

Where Are Mesa Graduates Headed?

Mesa claims that its first three postgraduate cohorts have produced around 300 alumni, who have joined more than 120 startups. The startup claims that its graduates take up roles across founders’ offices, product management, partnerships, account management and venture capital.

Agarwal claims that the experienced-professional postgraduate programme reports average salaries of ₹26-28 LPA. He also claimed that Mesa has so far incubated more than 50 student startups, which have clocked ₹50 Cr in annual revenue. The school also claims to provide equity-free grants and incubation support to student ventures.

This comes three years after Mesa last raised ₹34 Cr in a round led by Elevation Capital in 2023 to launch its startup leadership programme. Angel investors such as CRED’s Kunal Shah, Meesho’s Vidit Aatrey, and Urban Company’s Abhiraj Bahl also participated in the round.

Mesa operates in an emerging segment of alternative business education, competing most directly with Gurugram-based Masters’ Union, which combines industry-led management programmes with entrepreneurship support. Masters’ Union recently received full university status from the Haryana government. 

Other competitors in re-skilling and upskilling space include upGrad, Great Learning, Masai School, Eruditus and Springboard, among others.

item.title: Qualcomm Sells Shadowfax Shares Worth ₹157 Cr In Bulk Deal
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Early backer Qualcomm Ventures has sold 57.1 Lakh shares of listed logistics company Shadowfax via an open-market transaction for ₹157.3…
item.content:encoded:
Early backer Qualcomm Ventures has sold 57.1 Lakh shares of listed logistics company Shadowfax via an open-market transaction for ₹157.3 Cr.

According to BSE data, the chipmaker, via its affiliate Qualcomm Asia Pacific Pte Limited, sold the shares at ₹275.3 apiece to rake in the amount. This represented a discount of 6.6% against the stock’s last closing price on Monday.

Qualcomm Asia Pacific Pte Ltd owned 2.26% stake, or 1.32 Cr shares, in Shadowfax at the end of June 2026. However, the chipmaker then diluted some of this shareholding and sold 75 Lakh shares worth ₹183.9 Cr in August.

Qualcomm Ventures first invested in Shadowfax during the logistics company’s $22 Mn Series C round in 2018, alongside Mirae Asset and Eight Roads Ventures.

This is the latest bulk deal involving Shadowfax in recent months. Since August, private equity (PE) giant TPG has offloaded Shadowfax shares worth more than ₹700 Cr across multiple bulk deals. 

The bulk deals come as investors look to book profits amid a sharp uptick in Shadowfax’s stock prices. Shares of the logistics company have surged 29.3% in the past three months, and are up more than 122.91% in the last six months.

This jump has come on the back of healthy financial performance by the startup. The logistics major saw its consolidated net profit surge 8X to ₹65.4 Cr in Q1 FY27 as against ₹8 Cr in the year ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed 65% YoY and 10% QoQ to ₹1,358 Cr in the quarter under review.

Following the results, Shadowfax also revised its FY27 revenue growth forecast to 38-40%, a significant jump from the 28-30% guidance projected just a quarter ago.

Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Bansal and Vaibhav Khandelwal, Shadowfax operates a logistics network serving ecommerce, quick commerce and D2C brands. The company was listed on the stock exchanges earlier this year.

It currently operates across more than 16,372 pincodes and plans to increase its network of dark stores from 47 to 100 by March 2027 as it looks to strengthen its quick commerce business.

Shares of Shadowfax closed Monday’s trading session 0.12% lower at ₹294.75 on the BSE.

item.title: RDI Fund Announces First Cohort Of 19 Fund Managers, Eyes Deploying ₹7,131 Cr To Strengthen Deeptech Startups
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Central government-backed ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund has approved 19 second-level fund managers (SLFMs) with a…
item.content:encoded:
Central government-backed ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund has approved 19 second-level fund managers (SLFMs) with a total commitment of ₹7,131 Cr.

The Ministry of Science and Technology’s Empowered Group of Secretaries (EGoS) approved 14 alternative investment funds (AIFs) and five focused research organisations (FROs) for this purpose earlier this month, the ministry announced. 

The selected entities will channel capital from the RDI Fund to eligible technology enterprises undertaking research, development and innovation activities at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 4 and above.

The fund managers are also expected to mobilise private capital equivalent to the RDI Fund’s contribution, potentially expanding the pool of financing available to research-driven businesses.

Alongside approving the first cohort of fund managers, the EGoS approved five additional technologies for coverage under the RDI Fund. The government did not specify these technologies in its announcement.

The government said it would continue inviting applications and onboarding additional cohorts of fund managers, expanding the reach of the scheme and encouraging public-private investment in India’s research and innovation ecosystem.

Launched in November 2025, the RDI Scheme has an overall outlay of ₹1 Lakh Cr and aims to address the funding gap faced by companies developing high-risk, high-impact technologies. It is managed by an independent business unit housed within the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), under the Department of Science and Technology (DST).

The fund is designed to spur private investment in research-intensive businesses. However, its impact on investor sentiment, however, remains unclear. In August, The Indian Express reported that nearly two-thirds of the more than ₹2,000 Cr allocated to deeptech companies under the scheme had gone to firms linked to members of the panel involved in selecting beneficiaries. The report raised concerns about potential conflicts of interest.

Inc42’s Q3 2026 Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, which covered 85 institutional investors, found that 52% considered disclosure and recusal safeguards adequate, but said visibility into the process remained limited.

Another 25% viewed the issue as a governance failure that required independent oversight, while 14% said potential conflicts could be managed through disclosure and recusal. The remaining 9% said the issue was not a concern, arguing that the focus should be on selecting the right companies.

As per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’, deeptech startup funding in the September quarter zoomed 176% YoY to $290 Mn raised across 28 deals, compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in Q3 2025. The sector outpaced the broader startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn.

item.title: Nazara Top Deck Shuffle: Founder Mittersain Steps Down As MD; Caratlane’s Sacheti Takes Executive Role
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Listed gaming major Nazara Technologies announced a major leadership reshuffle today, highlighted by founder Nitish Mittersain stepping down as the…
item.content:encoded:
Listed gaming major Nazara Technologies announced a major leadership reshuffle today, highlighted by founder Nitish Mittersain stepping down as the company’s managing director. 

Mittersain, who founded the company in 1999 and took it public in 2021, has assumed a new role as “Founder and Non-Executive Director”. He will continue to provide strategic guidance to the board. 

Meanwhile, CaratLane founder Mithun Sacheti, who joined the board as an additional director earlier this year, has been elevated to an executive whole-time director role for a period of five years. Sacheti will now assume a new position to oversee strategic initiatives and take on some operational responsibilities. 

“He understands the consumer business space, digital consumer ecosystems … He brings extensive entrepreneurial,consumer and brand building experience,” the gaming major said in its disclosures to the bourses earlier today.

Besides, the board also noted the resignation of Rohit Sharma as Whole-time Director, effective from January 1, 2027, onwards, as he decided to pursue entrepreneurial opportunities. Sharma joined the company’s board as an advisor in January 2025 and was later roped in as executive director in August.

Additionally, Nazara’s CFO Rakesh Shah has also resigned to pursue external opportunities and will be replaced by Arun Agrawal, former global CFO at Ness Digital Engineering. Shah, who has been with the gaming major since 2010, will exit the company on October 15 though he will assist with transition duties for 90 days. 

The change at the top of Nazara’s hierarchy comes shortly after Mittersain exited as CEO amid a turning point in the listed company’s journey.

Back in March, Nazara acquired a 50% stake in Spanish casual gaming studio Bluetile Games and its associate BestPlay Systems for a deal worth $100.3 Mn at base value, with performance-linked earn-outs of up to $98.2 Mn. 

However, the terms of the deal were later restructured such that Nazara acquired 100% of Bluetile and BestPlay for a fixed cash consideration of $303 Mn, shelling out $89 Mn upfront and committing to pay the remainder in agreed tranches by April 1, 2027. 

Besides, the gaming giant also approved a ₹733.5 Cr fundraise via preferential issue of equity shares to the founders and senior leadership team of Bluetile and BestPlay, including Bluetile’s founder and CEO Raymond Stauffer, who also took over from Mittersain as CEO on September 1. 

Notably, Bluetile and BestPlay together generated nearly ₹1,400 Cr in revenue in calendar year 2025. Yet, Bluetile’s EBITDA remained flat in the quarter despite a 54% revenue jump as the company faced climbing user acquisition costs. 

Besides all this, the company also faced de-subsidiarisation of its gaming and esports media arm NODWIN Gaming this year. Nazara opted not to participate in a $100 Mn external funding round raised by NODWIN, resulting in its shareholding slipping below 51%. NODWIN is also seeking to list independently on the bourses in the near future. 

On the financial front, Nazara reported a net loss of ₹82.5 Cr on operating revenue of ₹428.8 Cr in Q1 FY27. The gaming major’s operating revenue also declined 14% YoY to ₹428.8 Cr.

item.title: Whizzo To Raise $26 Mn From Aavishkaar Capital, Bertelsmann
item.dc:creator: Debarghya Sil
item.description: Bengaluru-based Whizzo is in talks to raise around $26 Mn in its Series B funding round which could be co-led…
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based Whizzo is in talks to raise around $26 Mn in its Series B funding round which could be co-led by Aavishkaar Capital and Bertelsmann Investments (BI), Inc42 learnt.

As per sources, existing backers Fundamentum, Lightspeed Ventures, among others, are also likely to participate in the round. 

Questions sent to Whizzo didn’t elicit any response at the time of publication of the story. The article will be updated based on their responses.

The fresh round of funding comes almost six months after the startup raised around $15 Mn in its Series A funding round led by Fundamentum, with participation from Korean investor LB Investment Fund, and Lightspeed. Back then, the startup said it would utilise the funds for strengthening research and development of in-house IP for materials science innovation. Prior to this, Lightspeed Ventures led Whizzo’s seed round in 2025.

The Bengaluru-based startup raised its maiden institutional funding round in January 2025 to develop its advanced R&D capabilities, creation of a design lab for fashion-engineered textiles and the expansion of its supply chain.

Founded in 2024 by Shrestha Kukreja, Whizzo is a CDMO (contract development and manufacturing organisation) that offers textile design services and textile research & development services to clients across India, Vietnam, China and Bangladesh. 

The startup integrates R&D, formulation, prototyping, process engineering, and commercial-scale manufacturing under one roof. 

Whizzo works with B2B manufacturers and produces a wide range of materials for applications across geotextiles, agriculture textiles, protective and flame-retardant materials, specialty yarns, engineered apparel textiles, and industrial composites. It claims to combine sustainability with advanced materials science, offering proprietary textile blends. 

The potential fundraise comes amid continued investor interest in tech-led textile manufacturing and fabric innovation, as startups look to improve product development and manufacturing processes through proprietary materials and R&D capabilities.

item.title: [Update] Alpha Wave Ventures Sells Lenskart Shares Worth ₹1,705 Cr
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Update | October 12,  20:00 IST Lenskart early backer Alpha Wave Ventures has sold 2.64 Cr shares in a bulk deal…
item.content:encoded:
Update | October 12,  20:00 IST

Lenskart early backer Alpha Wave Ventures has sold 2.64 Cr shares in a bulk deal valuing the stock at ₹645.31 apiece. The investor raked in ₹1,704.8 Cr via the stake sale today. The details of the buyers couldn’t be immediately discerned.

Update| October 12, 17:48 IST

Shares of Lenskart ended today’s trading session 4.4% lower at ₹647.95 apiece on the BSE. Its market capitalisation stood at ₹1,12,698.3 Cr ($11.7 Bn) at the end of the day. The bearish momentum of the stock came after reports of early investor Alpha Wave Ventures stake sale surfaced.

As per reports, the VC firm plans to sell up to 1.6% of its stake in Lenskart for as much as ₹1,691 Cr, with the offer priced at a floor of ₹640 per share. The floor price is at a 5.6% discount to the stock’s closing price of ₹677.65 on October 9.

The proposed sale comprises 15.1 Mn shares, or a 0.9% stake, with an option to sell another 11.3 Mn shares, equivalent to 0.7%. If the investor sells the full 26.4 Mn shares on offer, its holding in Lenskart will fall to 1.82% from 3.42%.

The latest move adds to a series of stake sales by Lenskart’s early investors in recent months, with Alpha Wave itself having sold shares worth ₹1,856.8 Cr in August.

Early Investors Continue To Pare Holdings

In August, Alpha Wave Ventures sold 2.94 Cr Lenskart shares through multiple block deals at ₹630 apiece, according to NSE data. The transaction fetched the investor ₹1,856.8 Cr.

The shares were picked up by a mix of institutional investors, including the National Pension System (NPS) Trust, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, Bajaj Life Insurance, HDFC Life Insurance, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and Kuwait Investment Authority.

Alpha Wave Ventures held 3.42% of Lenskart, or around 5.9 Cr shares, at the end of June 2026. Its August sale reduced its holding by nearly 1.7 percentage points.

The proposed transaction comes amid a broader round of stake sales by investors in the company. SoftBank sold Lenskart shares worth ₹2,887.9 Cr, while Temasek offloaded a 2.05% stake for ₹1,934 Cr last month.

Earlier, in June, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority sold 4 Cr Lenskart shares in a block deal worth ₹1,960 Cr.

An extended bull run for the stock has provided a fertile ground for investors to cash in. The company’s stock has zoomed over 48% on a year-to-date basis on the back of robust financial performance of the stock.

On the financial front, Lenskart reported a 273% YoY surge in consolidated net profit to ₹228.4 Cr in Q1 FY27, up from ₹61.2 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, profit rose 12% from ₹203.6 Cr in the preceding quarter.

Operating revenue grew 43% YoY and 8% QoQ to ₹2,714.2 Cr. Including other income of ₹68.5 Cr, Lenskart’s total income stood at ₹2,782.7 Cr for the quarter.

item.title: PharmEasy Parent API Holdings’ FY26 Loss Declines 67% YoY To ₹520 Cr
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: PharmEasy parent API Holdings narrowed its consolidated net loss by 67% to ₹520 Cr in the fiscal year ended March…
item.content:encoded:
PharmEasy parent API Holdings narrowed its consolidated net loss by 67% to ₹520 Cr in the fiscal year ended March 2026 (FY26) from ₹1,572 Cr in the previous fiscal, with its operating revenue growing 12.7% YoY to ₹6,618.5 Cr.

The company attributed the improvement to its focus on customer experience, higher-value profitable segments, capacity utilisation, increasing wallet share and leveraging digital capabilities.

In its FY26 annual report, API Holdings said it improved margins by focusing on higher-margin products, particularly its private label brands, and optimising discounts in its B2R business.

Including other income of ₹70.8 Cr, the company’s total revenue stood at ₹6,689.2 Cr for FY26. However, it continued to report a loss before tax of ₹456.1 Cr.

In the first quarter of FY27, API Holdings reported a 10% YoY increase in revenue to ₹1,754 Cr  while EBITDA rose to ₹39.3 Cr. Gross margin improved to 21.4% from 19.9% in FY26, and EBITDA margin reached 2.2%. Its B2B business grew 8.2% YoY to ₹1,006 Cr revenue and turned EBITDA-positive at ₹70 lakh. 

The company said that PharmEasy’s B2C business posted ₹348 Cr revenue, with EBITDA losses narrowing to ₹17 Cr. Thyrocare reported 24% YoY revenue growth to ₹240 Cr, processed 5.4 Mn patients and conducted 55.2 Mn tests.

Where Did API Holdings Spend In FY26?

API Holdings’ consolidated expenses declined marginally by 0.9% to ₹7,146.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹7,208.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Purchases of stock-in-trade remained its largest expense, while lower employee benefit costs contributed to the overall reduction.

Purchases Of Stock-In-Trade: The expense rose 10.9% to ₹5,244.8 Cr from ₹4,729.6 Cr, accounting for about 73% of total expenses. The increase came as the company’s operating revenue expanded during the year.

Employee Benefit Expense: Employee costs fell 47.5% to ₹476.9 Cr from ₹908.4 Cr in FY25. A substantial part of the decline came from lower employee share-based payment expenses, which dropped to ₹62 Cr from ₹482.2 Cr in FY25.

Other Expenses: This category increased 7.5% YoY to ₹656.7 Cr from ₹610.7 Cr. Major components included ₹111.8 Cr of contractual payments to delivery associates, ₹73.4 Cr of sales promotion and marketing, ₹72.6 Cr of manpower charges, and ₹63.4 Cr of legal and professional fees.

API Holdings also reported a tax expense of ₹64.2 Cr, comprising ₹68 Cr in current tax, offset by a deferred tax credit of ₹4.2 Cr, and a prior-period charge of ₹0.4 Cr.

Products Account For 86% Of Revenue

API Holdings generates revenue from the sale of products and services. Product sales contributed ₹5,670 Cr, or 85.7% of revenue, in FY26. These include pharmaceutical, over-the-counter (OTC), surgical, consumable and private label products.

The company sources products from manufacturers and wholesalers and supplies them to local chemists, large pharmacies, doctors, clinics, online retailers on the PharmEasy platform and hospitals.

A significant part of this business flows through its chemist-focused distribution operations, while Aknamed supplies hospitals. The group also generates product revenue through collection kits sold by Thyrocare.

Services contributed ₹941.3 Cr, or 14.2% of revenue, in FY26. This includes diagnostics, teleconsulting, licensing and technology services.

Thyrocare’s diagnostic operations account for a substantial part of this stream, serving franchise partners, consumers, hospitals, diagnostic companies and independent phlebotomists. API Holdings also earns service revenue from diagnostic tests sold through the PharmEasy marketplace, fulfilment services and technology platforms, including Retailio, which connects pharmaceutical wholesalers and pharmacies.

How API Holdings’ Subsidiaries Contribute

Although API Holdings has six direct subsidiaries and 18 step-down subsidiaries, four businesses account for much of its activity across B2B distribution, diagnostics and consumer healthcare.

B2B: Ascent Wellness And Pharma Solutions, Aknamed

Ascent Wellness and Pharma Solutions supplies pharmaceutical products to chemists and institutions, sourcing directly from pharmaceutical companies and enabling retailers to place orders through a platform. Aknamed supplies hospitals with pharmaceutical products, consumables and surgical products sourced from pharmaceutical companies and distributors.

Together, the B2B businesses generated ₹4,082.4 Cr in revenue in FY26, with an EBITDA loss of ₹3.6 Cr. In Q1 FY27, they recorded combined revenue of ₹1,005.6 Cr and EBITDA of ₹70 Lakh.

Diagnostics: Thyrocare Technologies

Thyrocare, API Holdings’ listed diagnostics arm, is a key contributor to the group’s profitability. In FY26, it operated 41 laboratories, offered 1,275 tests, processed about 21 Cr tests and had more than 10,800 franchisees.

Its revenue grew 24% YoY to ₹240 Cr in Q1 FY27.

B2C: PharmEasy

PharmEasy operates the group’s consumer-facing healthcare marketplace. In FY26, the segment generated ₹1,334.5 Cr in revenue and reported an EBITDA loss of ₹44.1 Cr.

In Q1 FY27, it recorded revenue of ₹347.9 Cr, alongside an EBITDA loss of ₹17 Cr.

item.title: Brands Have A New Mission: How To Get AI To Say Your Name
item.dc:creator: Shraddha Goled
item.description: “Have you ever clicked your mouse HERE? You will.” That was the text accompanying the first banner ad on the…
item.content:encoded:
“Have you ever clicked your mouse HERE? You will.”

That was the text accompanying the first banner ad on the internet, launched by telecommunications company AT&T on HotWired.com in 1994. The ad reportedly clocked a 44% click-through rate in its first four months, a figure that would be extraordinary by the standards of almost any digital marketing channel today.

Over three decades, online advertising has evolved from banner ads to search, social media, programmatic buying, influencer marketing and performance marketing. 

Then, with the emergence of search engine optimisation (SEO) practices, brands started optimising websites, building backlinks, targeting keywords and creating content to improve their visibility. Over time, SEO grew into a $90 Bn industry. 

But the search box is now changing again.

Today, a growing number of consumers are turning to AI assistants instead of typing keywords into Google and opening a dozen links. Whether they are looking for accounting software, a nearby restaurant or the best smartphone under ₹50,000, they can simply ask an AI assistant for recommendations.

Their interaction with AI is no longer limited to a query or a list of results. Users/consumers ask follow-up questions, compare options, refine their requirements, and direct AI to recommend what they should buy.

This is where answer engine optimisation (AEO) and generative engine optimisation (GEO) have emerged as a new trend. But there is no single platform to optimise for, no standard ranking system and no clear way to measure success.

Much like what the SEO function was in its early days, marketers are still figuring out what works. Agencies are experimenting with how brands appear in answers generated by ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google’s AI-powered search products. They are tracking brand mentions, citations and recommendations, while trying to understand why one company gets surfaced over another.

But as brands scramble to show up in AI-generated answers, a bigger question is emerging: How can they ensure they are not just recommended by AI, but show up at the right moment? 

The Missing Link In AI Marketing

Currently, for brands, the challenge is not how to appear in AI answers but figure out whether that visibility brings more visitors, customers or sales.

Google historically gave marketers detailed visibility through tools such as Search Console and keyword-level paid search data. This model is considerably harder to replicate when consumers interact with AI through multi-step conversations.

AI platforms currently offer limited visibility into the prompts driving discovery. A user may start with a broad question, ask several follow-ups, compare products, and only then arrive at a purchase decision. For marketers, identifying which interaction influenced that journey is harder than attributing a click to a specific search query.

Organic visibility is also inconsistent across platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity. For queries around the “best” or “top” products and services, AI models may rely heavily on third-party publishers, reviews and user-generated content rather than brand websites.

As a result, brands need to build a consistent information ecosystem across websites, ads, influencers and third-party platforms.

“So, eventually, for optimising, it becomes a lot more important to produce content in the broader ecosystem. We often ask brands to be consistent with their communication,” said Rishabh Mahendru, senior vice president of client success and growth at AdLift.

Marketers are also grappling with how much control they have over their brands’ visibility in AI-driven discovery. AI platforms can answer users’ questions without sending them to an external website. These zero-click answers may be convenient for consumers, but they can reduce traffic to publisher and brand websites.

Even when AI search leads to a sale, tracing that purchase back to a specific interaction can be difficult. A consumer may discover a brand through an AI assistant, research it elsewhere and make a purchase days later. Traditional last-click attribution models may fail to capture the role AI played in that journey.

There is also less certainty around where and how brands appear. AI platforms determine which ads match a user’s intent, while changes in how models cite sources can make organic visibility unpredictable. Brands also risk appearing alongside misinformation, hate speech or polarising content in AI-generated responses. To address these, OpenAI is exploring geo-based ad experiments and brand-suitability pilots to give advertisers more insight into where their ads appear and how they perform.

Overall, with its ChatGPT Ads in India, OpenAI is bringing sponsored messages into conversations on the AI chatbot in one of its largest markets. Ads have been rolled out to users on Free and Go tiers, while Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Education users get an ad-free experience. More than 50 brands were planned to go live during the initial rollout, with WPP and Omnicom as OpenAI’s first agency partners in India. Businesses can access ChatGPT’s self-serve Ads Manager, with daily budgets starting at ₹725.

The Next Frontier Of Brand Visibility

With no standard way to measure AI search visibility or predict which brands will surface in AI-generated answers, startups are building tools to help businesses navigate the new landscape.

Antler-incubated RankinLLM, for instance, is building a GEO and AI search visibility platform. “We operate across three layers: an observability layer to track LLM activity, an intelligence layer to extract meaningful signals from noisy data, and an optimisation layer to fix identified gaps. Optimiser agents create a closed loop, while KPIs such as brand mentions, share of voice, citations and sentiment measure the impact,” said cofounder and CEO Kartik Sharma.

Bengaluru-based TruCommerce has taken a different approach. It initially built a tool to track how often brands appeared in AI-generated answers. But it found that much of the traffic coming from AI platforms was being wrongly counted as direct website visits. This led the startup to shift its focus to helping brands sell directly through AI platforms.

TruCommerce now connects brands’ product catalogues and inventory with AI assistants. This helps businesses track visitors coming from AI, make product information easier for AI tools to understand, and enable customers to buy products without leaving the conversation.

Meanwhile, Lightspeed-backed Gushwork helps small and medium-sized businesses attract potential customers through traditional search engines and AI tools. Its AI agents create content designed to appear in search results, while its platform tracks the enquiries this content generates.

Other startups, including Nexad, Parsnip and AdCreative AI, are also building tools to help brands advertise and improve their visibility across AI platforms.

For marketers, however, this shift is still in its early stages. Traditional SEO took decades to develop its tools, metrics and best practices. AI is at the same crossroads.

India’s deeptech startups raised substantially more capital in Q3 2026, even as the number of deals edged lower. 

As per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals, compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in Q3 2025. The 176% YoY increase outpaced the broader startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn.

For context, deeptech startups are the ones that develop advanced technologies and hardware and include innovations across sub-segments like spacetech, robotics, defence technology and semiconductors.

Large Spacetech Rounds Drive Deeptech Funding Surge

The sharp rise in funding, despite a marginal decline in deal count, points to a concentration of capital in a smaller pool of startups. 

In this, large spacetech rounds accounted for a significant share of the funding deployed during the quarter, with the startups in the sector netting $130 Mn, accounting for about 45% of deeptech funding in Q3. Six-year-old spacetech startup Pixxel’s $100 Mn round was one of four mega funding rounds recorded during the quarter. The round accounted for over three-fourths of the segment’s total.

Sustaining this momentum will require capital to reach beyond a select group of companies. As per a recent report by the Indian Venture and Alternate Capital Association (IVCA), deeptech startups continue to face a funding gap at the Series B and C stages, with few funds equipped to write the larger cheques needed to take technologies from development to commercial scale.

IVCA President Rajat Tandon said bridging this gap, deepening domestic limited partner participation, and improving exit pathways will be critical to building globally competitive deeptech companies.

“India’s deeptech opportunity is moving from promise to more investible commitments, with an increasingly institutionalised ecosystem play. The growth in capital flowing into deeptech over the past decade reflects the confidence investors have in India’s scientific and technological capabilities. However, taking deeptech startups and entrepreneurs from the laboratory to global scale will require capital that is patient, appropriately structured, and available across the entire growth journey,” he said.

Government Push Adds To Deeptech Funding Momentum

Bharat Innovation Fund cofounder and partner Ashwin Raguraman attributed some of the recent momentum to the government’s ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund and its wider push to support technology-led businesses.

“I attribute (growth in deeptech funding) this quarter and maybe even last quarter predominantly due to the announcement on the government’s deeptech-focused ₹1 Lakh Cr RDI Fund and a fairly solid government push, which is making capital available to VC funds,” Raguraman told Inc42.

The RDI Fund aims to catalyse private investment in research-intensive businesses. Its framework includes eligibility requirements for R&D-intensive technologies at technology readiness level (TRL) 4 or above, indicating that they have progressed beyond basic laboratory validation.

New investment vehicles also emerged during the quarter. Asiana Fund and JC Capital jointly launched a ₹1,000 Cr deeptech fund, while Transition VC and Accel launched funds to back technology-led businesses.

Access Free Report

RDI Fund Faces Questions Over Governance

However, the extent to which the RDI Fund has influenced investor sentiment remains uncertain. In August, The Indian Express reported that nearly two-thirds of the more than ₹2,000 Cr allocated to deeptech companies under the scheme had gone to firms with links to members of the panel involved in selecting beneficiaries, raising concerns over potential conflicts of interest.

Inc42’s Q3 2026 Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, which covered 85 institutional investors, found that 52% considered disclosure and recusal safeguards adequate but said visibility remained limited. 

Another 25% viewed the issue as a governance failure requiring independent oversight, while 14% said such investment ties could be managed through disclosure and recusal. The remaining 9% said it was not a concern, arguing that the focus should remain on company selection.

The findings suggest that the availability of government-backed capital is only part of the equation. Transparency in its allocation and the availability of patient capital across funding stages will also shape the sector’s ability to turn promising technologies into globally competitive businesses.

item.title: D2C Brand Boldfit Raises ₹400 Cr From Bharat Value Fund For Retail Expansion
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: D2C fitness and sportswear brand Boldfit has raised around ₹400 Cr (about $41.8 Mn) from Bharat Value Fund as part…
item.content:encoded:
D2C fitness and sportswear brand Boldfit has raised around ₹400 Cr (about $41.8 Mn) from Bharat Value Fund as part of its Series B funding round.

The fund is a Category II AIF managed by The Wealth Company Alternates, part of Pantomath Group.

Boldfit said the investment would support nationwide retail expansion, product innovation, and manufacturing. It also plans to pursue selective acquisitions to strengthen its presence and capabilities across categories.

Founded in 2018 by Pallav Bihani, Bengaluru-based Boldfit sells performance sportswear, athletic footwear, sports equipment, and fitness essentials. The startup claims to serve more than 2 Cr customers annually across India.

“We’re building a deeply integrated sports business, investing in product innovation, manufacturing excellence and nationwide retail to create the scale and capabilities required to serve India’s sporting ambitions,” Bihani said.

The retail push builds on plans outlined during its ₹110 Cr funding round from Bessemer Venture Partners in November 2024, when Boldfit said it intended to open offline stores over the following 12-18 months.

Following the latest round, Boldfit’s total funding to date has risen to over ₹510 Cr. The startup also counts cricketer KL Rahul and former tennis player Sania Mirza among its investors.

India’s fitness and sports goods market is estimated to be worth $16 Bn and is projected to reach $35 Bn by FY31, driven by rising disposable incomes, growing health awareness, and wider access through ecommerce, organised retail, and quick commerce channels.

As a result, Indian sportswear and athleisure startups are seeing a lot of investor interest. In June, sportswear startup Agilitas raised ₹225 Cr funding round from Nexus Venture Partners and Rainmatter, with Nexus investing ₹200 Cr and Rainmatter contributing ₹25 Cr.

In January, D2C athleisure brand CAVA announced a ₹40 Cr Series A round led by Sharrp Ventures, with participation from V3 Ventures and existing investor Spring Marketing Capital.

item.title: How XSCACE Is Taking On Bose And B&O With 12mm-Thin Speakers
item.dc:creator: Inc42 Staff
item.description: For decades, names like Bose, Marshall, Bang & Olufsen and KEF have shaped how the world listens to music. Their…
item.content:encoded:
For decades, names like Bose, Marshall, Bang & Olufsen and KEF have shaped how the world listens to music. Their dominance was built on one simple premise: better sound came from bigger hardware, larger cabinets, larger drivers and speakers designed to be seen and admired.

But that premise is increasingly getting at odds with how modern spaces are being designed today. Architects and homeowners are favouring clean walls, minimal interiors and technology that fits seamlessly into the room instead of dominating it.

The shift has put one of consumer electronics’ oldest categories in a difficult spot: speakers. Good quality speakers need physical space to deliver the depth, power and clarity that listeners expect. Manufacturers have tried to shrink the hardware, but making it smaller meant compromising on sound quality that made the product desirable in the first place — a trade-off the industry has largely lived with rather than solved.

For Utkarsh Hora, the cofounder of Canadian architectural audio startup XSCACE, audio was part of his family history. His grandfather, Bansi Lal Hora, had worked with Philips in Thailand before returning to India, where he began repairing high-end audio equipment. His father, Manoj Hora, carried that experience forward, building a business around premium audio installations. For Utkarsh, speakers and audio systems were therefore less a hobby than a part of everyday life.

During his time at the University of Toronto, he began wondering whether high-performance audio really needed to take up so much space. The question eventually became the starting point for XSCACE, which Utkarsh founded in 2022. He set out to build speakers that could deliver high-quality sound without taking over a room or compromising its design. 

The challenge, however, was rooted in a fundamental constraint of speaker design known as Hoffman’s Iron Law. According to the law, a designer can optimise for only two of three things at once: deep bass, a small enclosure and high efficiency. XSCACE’s challenge was to push the boundaries of that trade-off without compromising the quality of sound. 

After two years of development and testing, XSCACE made its first commercial sale in January 2024. Today, the brand has a range of ultra-compact speakers built around six proprietary technologies. It is expanding its distribution across international markets.

 

How XSCACE Is Reinventing The Wheel 

When Utkarsh started his entrepreneurial journey, he observed that modern luxury spaces were becoming increasingly minimal. Architects and interior designers wanted clean walls, hidden wiring and fewer visible fixtures. 

Speakers, however, remained stubbornly hard to hide. In-wall and in-ceiling speakers existed, but they often came with a compromise. Products that blended into the architecture could fall short on sound, while speakers built for stronger performance typically needed more space.

The fundamental challenge stemmed from a long-standing principle of speaker design known as Hoffman’s Iron Law. It describes the trade-off between a speaker’s size, bass response and efficiency. Improving one typically means giving up something elsewhere.

Rather than accept the rules as they were, the founder began by rethinking what sat at the speaker’s centre: the driver. In a sense, Utkarsh was trying to reinvent the wheel.

Instead of optimising individual components in isolation, XSCACE approached the speaker as one interconnected system. Driver geometry, motor design, cone materials, crossover architecture, cabinet construction and thermal management were developed together, with each element designed to work within the constraints of the others.

“We didn’t eliminate the trade-off altogether but became far more intentional about where it exists,” the founder said.

This paved the way for the foundation of six proprietary technologies, each tackling a different part of the performance equation. These are as follows:

  • Nano Resonance: To focus on ultra-compact driver performance
  • PowerDense Dynamics: Extracts higher output from miniature motors
  • AeroFrame Chassis: Reduces resonance
  • PrecisionXover Array: Solves for seamless driver integration
  • XS-Flow: For Airflow and bass response
  • PsySculpt: Creates a more convincing spatial experience through psychoacoustic tuning

“Among these, Nano Resonance was one of the hardest pieces to develop,” the founder said, adding that the challenge was to get deep bass, high output and low distortion from a miniature driver while maintaining long-term reliability. 

From Prototype To Production

A prototype that performs exceptionally in controlled conditions does not automatically translate into a product that can be manufactured consistently. So the next big task was to turn that engineering into a product that could be manufactured consistently without losing performance. 

The founder had to revisit parts of the product with manufacturability and repeatability in mind.

“It’s one thing to build a prototype and altogether a different ball game to build the exact same product at scale,” he said.

While spending on simulation, prototyping, testing and refinement across acoustics, mechanical design, materials and manufacturing, the founder had to build a multidisciplinary team and invest in engineering capabilities.

After rigorous experimentation, testing and improving the designs, the founder was finally able to turn its two products, Bonsai and Cane, from early experimental concepts into actual products that were ready to be manufactured and sold.

  • Bonsai: An ultra-slim, compact speaker that is just 12 mm deep and delivers 40W. It is designed to be mounted discreetly on walls or installed in walls or ceilings.
  • Cane: A slightly larger 23 mm-thin slim-array speaker with 50W output, designed for spaces where you want more output while keeping the speaker visually unobtrusive.

Building More Than Speakers

Utkarsh’s quest didn’t end with making speakers compact and minimal. From the outset, he saw software as an extension of his product lineup.

“I did not want our products to depend entirely on third-party software,” he said.

Therefore, he started developing an in-house software ecosystem. Today, the brand offers an AI Configurator to help architects, designers and integrators plan and configure audio systems, alongside a companion app for users and the Xylem DSP Controller, which lets installers fine-tune sound based on a room’s acoustics. 

Over time, the AI Configurator is expected to become more than a planning tool. Utkarsh sees it evolving into a broader platform that can support installation, calibration, optimisation and ongoing system management. The software strategy also reflects where he wants to take XSCACE as a business.

“Our five-year vision is to establish XSCACE as a global reference in premium architectural audio,” he said, adding that broader plans include expanding beyond loudspeakers into software, DSP, amplification and complementary products, while strengthening its presence in India and expanding across the US, Europe and the Middle East.

For him, growth is not just about revenue or entering more markets. He measures the brand’s progress through its engineering, intellectual property, product consistency and the trust it builds with architects, integrators and customers.

In many ways, that brings XSCACE back to the problem that started it.

The brand did not set out simply to build smaller speakers. It wanted to challenge the assumption that high-performance audio had to remain visible.

Now, as XSCACE moves from compact architectural speakers towards a broader audio ecosystem, the original idea remains at the centre of the brand: build small, think big and make every inch punch above its weight.

item.title: Hero Electronix-Owned Tessolve Secures $75 Mn To Expand Semiconductor Capabilities
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Hero Electronix-owned Tessolve Semiconductor raised $75 Mn (₹718 Cr) in a funding round led by Vector Line Capital, with additional…
item.content:encoded:
Hero Electronix-owned Tessolve Semiconductor raised $75 Mn (₹718 Cr) in a funding round led by Vector Line Capital, with additional participation from existing backers TPG and Novo Tellus Capital Partners.

The fresh capital will support acquisitions that complement its existing capabilities, broaden its service offerings and strengthen its international business. 

The company is already in advanced discussions to close multiple acquisitions over the next couple of quarters. It last acquired Germany’s Dream Chip Technologies GmbH (DCT) in a ₹400 Cr deal back in November 2024.

“This investment will support acquisitions that further strengthen our offerings, and Vector Line’s focus on the sector and their relationships will add significant value,” Tessolve cofounder and chief executive Srini Chinamilli said.

Founded in 2004 by Chinamilli, P Raja Manickam and Veerappan V, Tessolve provides end-to-end semiconductor engineering services, spanning chip architecture and design, validation, testing and embedded systems.

The company is designing AI and HPC chips by leveraging its in-house pre-engineered semiconductor platforms and design flows to shorten development cycles, alongside a global lab infrastructure and partnerships with leading foundries, IP, EDA and test equipment companies.

Tessolve claims to have worked with leading hyperscalers and 18 of the world’s top 20 semiconductor companies. 

Hero Electronix, the electronics and tech arm of Hero Group, acquired a controlling stake in the semiconductor company in 2016,  with plans to complete a phased acquisition of a significant majority holding by the end of that year.

“Two decades ago we started with silicon test engineering. Today we are designing and productising complete chips for the companies building AI infrastructure,” Chinamilli said.

Tessolve last raised $150 Mn in a fresh round in 2025, led by TPG Growth. With the latest infusion, the startup’s cumulative funding stands at $265 Mn.

The development comes amid broader momentum in India’s deeptech sector, where semiconductor and chip design startups have drawn rising investor interest.

This increasing investor interest is also supported by the government’s ₹1.25 Lakh Cr India Semiconductor Mission 2.0, which was launched with an aim to build the country’s chip design and manufacturing ecosystem.

Some examples of this include AI-native semiconductor verification startup VerifAIX’s $5 Mn seed funding round in September, HrdWyr $13 Mn Series A funding round, among others.

Broader investor interest for advanced hardware and tech startups in India, which includes robotics, semiconductors and aerial vehicles, rose 176% YoY to $290 Mn, as per Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026.

item.title: BYJU’S Parent To Hold 32% Stake In Aakash After Settlement: Report
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Think & Learn Pvt Ltd (TLPL), the insolvent parent of BYJU’s, is set to hold around 32% in Aakash Educational…
item.content:encoded:
Think & Learn Pvt Ltd (TLPL), the insolvent parent of BYJU’s, is set to hold around 32% in Aakash Educational Services once a settlement resolving its long-running shareholding dispute with the coaching company is fully implemented.

According to an ET report, the stake will be higher than the roughly 25.75% TLPL held before Aakash’s ₹240 Cr rights issue became the subject of litigation last year. TLPL’s recorded shareholding fell sharply after Aakash withheld a portion of the shares it had subscribed for.

The settlement will include allotment of rights issue shares as well as transfer of existing shares to TLPL, the report said, adding that there would be no cash consideration for the deal between TLPL, Aakash, and the coaching institute’s investor Manipal Group.

Aakash and Manipal Group declined to comment on Inc42’s queries regarding the development.

This comes a month after the Bengaluru bench of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) directed TLPL’s resolution professional (RP) and successful bidder Comprint Tech Solutions (India) to maintain status quo on assets auctioned by TLPL amid a dispute over their ownership.

The Tribunal’s order followed claims by the RP of another BYJU’s group entity, BYJU’s K3 Education, that goods worth around ₹150 Cr had been auctioned for about ₹16 Cr. K3’s RP argued that the company had a substantial stake in the assets and that their further disposal could leave it without assets to continue its corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP).

TLPL’s RP disputed the claim, arguing that TLPL had procured the hardware and owned the educational content stored on the devices. The NCLT observed that neither side had produced sufficient documentary evidence to conclusively establish ownership.

The Tribunal directed Comprint to submit an inventory of the purchased assets, photographs and their storage address. TLPL’s RP was also asked to provide details of the assets, their valuation and the auction process. The NCLT has not cancelled the auction or made a final determination on ownership.

The dispute stems from separate insolvency proceedings against TLPL and K3 Education. TLPL entered insolvency proceedings in July 2024 after the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) approached the tribunal over unpaid sponsorship dues of around ₹159 Cr.

K3 Education is facing a separate insolvency process following a Section 9 petition filed by operational creditor Kritikal Solutions.

Last month, Byju Raveendran reportedly proposed relinquishing his claimed beneficial interest in 17.89 Mn Aakash shares to settle Qatar Holding’s arbitration claim of over $235 Mn against him.

The shares, held through Singapore-based Beeaar Investco Pte, represent about 5.7% of Aakash’s equity. They were acquired in 2022 using $150 Mn in financing extended by Qatar Holding, owned by the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), to Raveendran’s Singapore-based investment vehicle, BYJU’s Investments Pte Ltd (BIPL). Raveendran personally guaranteed the financing.

Qatar Holding terminated the financing agreement after alleging defaults by BIPL and demanded more than $235 Mn, including early termination fees and penalties. It also alleged that the Aakash shares had been transferred to Beeaar, which it claims is beneficially owned by Raveendran, in violation of the agreement.

The proposed settlement involving Aakash shares could affect the coaching company’s ownership structure and Qatar Holding’s recovery efforts. However, the settlement terms and the extent to which they would address the fund’s claims remain unclear.

B2B manufacturing company Zetwerk has set a price band of ₹143-₹151 per share for its IPO, which will be worth ₹5,012.3 Cr at the upper end of the band.

The issue comprises a fresh issue of ₹2,830 Cr and an OFS of up to 14.45 Cr shares, worth ₹2,182.3 Cr at the upper end, according to its RHP.

The IPO will open for subscription on October 15 and close on October 19. Anchor investor bidding will take place on October 14.

At the upper end of the price band, Zetwerk is seeking a post-issue market capitalisation of around ₹25,583 Cr (about $2.7 Bn).

The company has increased the fresh issue from ₹2,600 Cr outlined in its UDRHP. The OFS has also grown 49.2% from about 9.7 Cr shares.

Promoters and cofounders Amrit Pratik Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan will each sell up to 1.42 Cr shares. Other selling shareholders include promoter group entity Creovate Innovation and funds associated with Peak XV Partners, Accel India, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Kae Capital.

Zetwerk plans to use ₹2,160 Cr from the fresh issue to repay or prepay borrowings of the company and certain subsidiaries. The remaining net proceeds will fund acquisitions and general corporate purposes.

Zetwerk filed its draft IPO papers confidentially in March, followed by its UDRHP in August.

Inside Zetwerk’s Business Model

Founded in 2018, Zetwerk operates a manufacturing platform serving businesses across industrial and consumer goods categories.

It combines capacity from third-party suppliers and its own facilities to manage manufacturing orders across sectors including renewable energy, consumer electronics, aerospace, defence, oil and gas, and industrial automation.

Its customers include Siemens Gamesa, Acer India, boAt, NTPC Renewable Energy, CG Power and Industrial Solutions, and the Indian Air Force.

As of June 30, Zetwerk operated 26 manufacturing facilities across India, the US, Germany, and Spain.

It entered the unicorn club in 2021 after raising $150 Mn. It has raised over $900 Mn in funding to date from investors like Peak XV Partners, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Accel India, Greenoaks Capital Partners, and D1 Capital Partners.

In July, Inc42 reported that Zetwerk had raised ₹500 Cr from Bharat Value Fund ahead of its IPO. Its RHP confirmed that shares worth ₹500 Cr were allotted to Bharat Value Fund and Bharat Value Fund – Series III on April 2.

Revenue Grows, Losses Persist

On the financial front, Zetwerk’s operating revenue increased 40.4% to ₹15,913.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹11,331.9 Cr in FY25. However, its net loss, including discontinued operations, widened to ₹1,606.2 Cr from ₹370.7 Cr.

The FY26 loss included a ₹796.4 Cr exceptional charge linked to changes in share conversion ratios and a ₹453 Cr impairment charge in its discontinued civil infrastructure business.

For Q1 FY27, operating revenue from continuing operations rose 55.4% to ₹4,117.9 Cr from ₹2,649.4 Cr in Q1 FY26. Its total net loss narrowed 46.4% to ₹733 Cr from ₹1,368.5 Cr in the year-ago period.

Of the latest quarterly loss, ₹668.9 Cr came from discontinued operations, while continuing operations accounted for ₹64.1 Cr. The year-ago quarter included ₹803.2 Cr in exceptional charges from continuing operations and the ₹453 Cr impairment charge in the discontinued business.

Separately, Zetwerk and US-based transformer startup Ayr Energy reached a settlement in September, agreeing to withdraw pending claims in US and Indian courts and jointly seek termination of a related US International Trade Commission investigation.

Zetwerk had accused Ayr Energy founder Anirudh Reddy, a former senior executive at the manufacturing platform, of misusing confidential information and trade secrets. Ayr Energy had filed counterclaims against Zetwerk, which disputed the allegations.

Zetwerk’s IPO follows public market debuts of new-age tech companies like RentoMojo, Moneyview, Shiprocket, LEAP India, and ESDS Software this year.

item.title: Tonbo Imaging Sets IPO Price Band At ₹665-₹700 For ₹852 Cr Issue
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma

item.content:encoded:
Defence tech company Tonbo Imaging India has set a price band of ₹665-₹700 per equity share for its ₹852.1 Cr OFS-only IPO.

The IPO comprises an OFS of up to 1.22 Cr equity shares, with no fresh issue component.

At the upper end of the price band, the IPO values the company at ₹4,009.8 Cr (about $480 Mn).

The issue will open for subscription on October 15 and close on October 19, with anchor investor bidding scheduled for October 14.

The selling shareholders include promoters and cofounders Arvind Kondangi Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza, alongside investors such as CEAQ Technologies and Artiman Partners.

The offer has been reduced from the 1.81 Cr shares proposed in its draft papers. SEBI issued its observations on its DRHP last month, after the company refiled the draft papers in August.

Founded in 2003, Tonbo initially provided R&D and technology development services as a subsidiary of a research company. Following its buyout by the promoters in 2012, it shifted to manufacturing defence products, including advanced electro-optic and electronic systems.

Currently, the company designs and develops defence electronics and imaging systems used for surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting and other military applications. Its product portfolio includes thermal imaging systems, weapon sights, handheld thermal imaging binoculars, driver-vision systems, targeting equipment, fire-control systems and missile seekers.

Tonbo is also developing newer defence products, including a loitering munition and a high-power microwave-based anti-drone system called WaveStrike.

As of June 30, 2026, the startup had deployed more than 28,000 systems across 24 countries

In April last year, Tonbo raised ₹175 Cr in a Series D funding round from investors including Florintree Advisors, Tenacity Ventures, and EXIM Bank at a reported valuation of ₹1,500 Cr.

Tonbo follows an asset-light manufacturing model, outsourcing production to certified electronics manufacturing services partners such as Kaynes Technology and Avalon Technology. Prototype development, system integration and qualification testing are undertaken in-house. 

On the financial front, Tonbo reported operating revenue of ₹36 Cr and a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr in Q1 FY27. For the fiscal ended in March 2026, its revenue from operations declined 22.7% to ₹362.6 Cr from ₹ 469.1 Cr in FY25. Net profit declined 43% YoY to ₹50.8 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹72.8 Cr in the previous year.

item.title: Pledge, Sell, Pledge Again: Bhavish Agarwal & Ola Electric’s Dilemma
item.dc:creator: Bismah Malik
item.description: For close to two years, Bhavish Aggarwal has been stuck between a rock and a hard place. All to keep…
item.content:encoded:
For close to two years, Bhavish Aggarwal has been stuck between a rock and a hard place. All to keep Ola Electric and his other ventures going without giving up control of the company he built. 

Between November 2024 and March 2025, Aggarwal pledged Ola Electric shares to raise debt for Krutrim Data Centre, the AI infrastructure and services company that he founded in 2023. 

Then in December 2025, he sold part of his stake in Ola Electric to repay the ₹260 Cr loan that covered the pledge and release the encumbered shares, selling 3.93% of his holding in the company. 

At the time, Ola Electric said repaying the loan meant the company should operate with zero pledge overhang. But ten months later, another pledge is here. 

On 30 September, Aggarwal pledged 20 Cr Ola Electric shares, or 4.32% of the company, against non-convertible debentures (NCDs) issued by Krutrim Data Centre. 

CTL Trusteeship holds the pledge on behalf of the debenture holders. 

Neither the filings nor Ola have disclosed how much Krutrim Data Centre is raising through these debentures.

What is clear is that this is a bigger pledge than before — 20 Cr shares (4.32%) against 17.3 Cr shares (3.93%) that secured a ₹260 Cr loan in the previous instance.

Ola Electric said that the pledge is solely meant to fund his subscription to the company’s upcoming ₹1,000 Cr rights issue, and that no shares are being sold, and that Aggarwal will invest on the same terms as every other shareholder

Shriram Subramanian, founder of advisory firm InGovern Research, said that the EV firm scores poorly on what investors call the “say-do” ratio: how often a company does what it says. The situation around the pledges highlights this. 

He added that investors will read a founder pledging, clearing and pledging again as a sign of stress for the promoter or the promoter’s group entities, “and that may not be a good sign.”

Especially after Ola raised ₹780 Cr through a qualified institutional placement (QIP) in June 2026. Four months later, it is asking shareholders for more. 

Ola Electric’s Cash Problem

One thing we need to point out: Ola Electric’s rights issue is coming on the heels of the improved operating metrics. Market share rose from 5.1% in Q4 FY26 to 8.4% in Q1 FY27, but short of the 15–20% it targeted for 2026. 

But in the same quarter, rival Ather delivered 83,173 scooters, more than twice Ola’s 39,192, while posting a lower loss. 

Ola’s dealership rollout is still under way, and its gigafactory has not yet reached its 6 GWh target. Both are drags on its bottom line. 

In Q1 FY27, Ola Electric reported revenue of ₹455 Cr, down 45% from a year earlier and below its own guidance of ₹500–550 Cr. Its net loss narrowed to ₹336 Cr, the lowest in seven quarters, but free cash flow was still negative at about ₹351 Cr.

At that rate, the ₹780 Cr raised in June covers roughly two quarters of cash burn. The rights issue, approved by the board on 28 September, would add up to ₹1,000 Cr.

According to the draft letter of offer, about ₹350 Cr will go towards repaying or prepaying borrowings and ₹400 Cr towards organic growth. Of the money earmarked so far, nearly half goes to paying down debt.

These are partly paid shares, which means investors pay in installments. The issue price, entitlement ratio and payment schedule are yet to be announced.

The Idea Behind Pledging Instead Of Selling

A rights issue is offered only to existing shareholders, in proportion to what they already own. Aggarwal still holds roughly 26.2% of Ola Electric shareholding.

If he sits out this rights issue and does not buy in, his stake and therefore his control will shrink. 

According to the legal experts we spoke to, Agarwal also cannot simply borrow debt from Ola Electric. Section 67(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 bars a public company from giving financial assistance, directly or indirectly, through a loan, guarantee or security, for anyone to buy or subscribe to its own shares.

Selling shares to invest in the rights issue would be counterproductive to Aggarwal’s goal of maintaining his stake in the company, so pledging shares is the only option on the table  

The money comes through Krutrim Data Centre, which, as a company, can issue debentures in a way an individual cannot. Aggarwal has used this route before, with the same company and the same kind of pledge.

What has changed since is his priority. 

In December, he faced a similar choice and went the other way. 

With the stock near a record low at that time and his pledged shares closer to a margin call, he sold part of his stake to repay the loan and release the pledged shares. 

A margin call on pledged shares would have meant that Aggarwal would have had to deposit funds or securities to cover for the dropping market value of the pledged collateral. 

Aggarwal avoided this eventuality by selling a portion of his stake in December 2025, but now he is looking at pledging shares to protect his stake. For now at least, it would seem that retaining his control on Ola Electric matters more than any overhang from the pledge.

The Krutrim Link

The current shares pledged by Agarwal aim to secure debt on behalf of  Krutrim Data Centre. That also puts a private company’s balance sheet directly behind a listed company’s shares. 

If, for instance, Krutrim Data Centre struggles to repay these NCDs, the pledged Ola Electric shares are exposed, and could be sold by the lender group, even if Ola Electric has recovered financially. 

InGovern Research’s Subramanian said that if Krutrim’s debt goes bad and the lender enforces the pledge, it could sell the shares, which would weigh on the stock.

He called this an extreme scenario, but said the risk alone is an overhang: public investors will keep watching whether Krutrim is able to pay back the debt. But the lender has to give reasonable notice, sell, and return any surplus, and Aggarwal can redeem the shares until then. 

It is also not clear how the money raised by Krutrim reaches Agarwal, whether as a loan, an advance or in some other form, or whether all of it is meant for the rights issue.

That route of funds transfer from Krutrim to Agarwal also matters, according to VPS Law Associates’s VP Singh.

He says that under Section 185 of the Companies Act, a straight loan from Krutrim to Agarwal is not applicable, however it could be a likely scenario of Krutrim repaying some loan it already owes to Agarwal or Krutrim directly subscribing to Ola Electric rights issue through entitlements Aggarwal renounces in its favour. 

For Ola Electric itself, this would not be a related-party question. “A transaction only between Krutrim and Aggarwal does not automatically become an Ola Electric related-party transaction. That will kick in when Ola Electric or its subsidiaries deal with a related party,” Singh added.

In the scenario that the lenders decided to enforce the pledge, Ola Electric’s board would have no say. “The shares are the promoter’s property and freely transferable; the company’s obligation is only confined to disclosure,” Singh said. 

Can Falling Stock Trigger A Crisis? 

A pledge is a loan secured by shares, and the value of that security moves with the stock price. That is exactly what makes it a double-edged arrangement.

At around ₹37 a share, the 20 Cr pledged shares by Agarwal are worth roughly ₹740 Cr. 

Brokerages like Citi have set a target price of ₹26 for the next 12 months, indicating that investors should sell. 

Lenders in a pledge arrangement typically respond to a price fall by asking the borrower to pledge more shares. If the promoter cannot provide them, lenders can sell the pledged shares in the market.

That is likely to result in a runaway effect where the price is pushed down further, triggering the call  for more shares or more funds to cover the pledge. 

Subramanian elaborated, but he stressed that this is an extreme scenario. “If Ola’s stock keeps falling, the value of the pledged shares drops against the margin the lender requires. So more and more shares would have to be pledged. Either the promoter pledges more shares to hold the margin, or investors sell their shares to recover some money, which adds to the downward spiral,”

Ola Electric’s investors have already seen a version of this. When Aggarwal sold shares in December to clear his earlier pledge, the stock fell 11% in two days and came close to its record low. 

Ola Electric’s stock has fallen about 30% over the past year and trades at less than half its IPO price of ₹76.

While legally, there is no law that bars Agarwal from pledging the shares in a listed firm to secure debt for his private company, the cost he and Ola Electric pay is of credibility. The share entitlements to key shareholders and the schedule of funds payments will all be keenly watched out for.

After that, the question is purely operational in nature. Ola needs to bring its quarterly cash burn down before the money from the QIP and the rights issue runs out. 

If Ola Electric needs to raise money again, Agarwal will face the same choice between selling and borrowing, and the cycle will begin anew. 

MARKETS WATCH: NEW ISSUES, POST-IPO JOURNEY & MORE

Snapdeal Parent AceVector Lists At 11.6% Discount: AceVector debuted on the BSE at ₹28.30 on October 5, against its IPO price of ₹32, and closed the day 18.4% below the issue price at ₹26.10. Its market cap at close stood at ₹1,420.3 Cr, versus an IPO valuation of ₹1,741.4 Cr.

ideaForge CEO Pledges 2.8 Lakh Shares: Promoter and CEO Ankit Mehta pledged 0.56% of the drone maker’s share capital, worth about ₹20.56 Cr, in favour of Infina Finance for “personal financial requirements”. The pledge comes months after ideaForge raised ₹500 Cr via a QIP in July.

Peak XV Halves Awfis Stake Via ₹30 Cr Bulk Deal: Peak XV sold 12.2 lakh Awfis shares at ₹245 apiece, offloading more than half of the 3.24% stake it held at the end of June. Awfis closed Friday 3.7% higher at ₹247.15, near its 52-week low of ₹229.55.

FirstCry’s Swara Baby Products Gets SEBI Nod For ₹1,000 Cr IPO: The Brainbees Solutions subsidiary has secured the markets regulator’s approval for its proposed ₹1,000 Cr public issue.

AITMC Files Updated DRHP: The agri-drone company has filed its UDRHP for a fresh issue of up to 3.5 Cr shares, about ten months after receiving SEBI’s nod. It reported a ₹13.4 Cr profit in FY26 on revenue of ₹106.8 Cr.

StockGro Parent Files Confidential DRHP: AssetGro Fintech is targeting an IPO of up to ₹2,500 Cr, including an ₹800 Cr fresh issue, even as StockGro raises $10.4 Mn in a Series B led by BITKRAFT Ventures.

That’s all for this week.

EVs Power Cleantech Funding Boom

India’s cleantech story accelerated in Q3 2026. The quarter saw the sector nearly triple its funding volume on the back of big-ticket electric mobility rounds and rising deal activity. So, what’s pulling investors towards the sector and can the momentum extend beyond EVs?

The Cleantech Boom: As per Inc42 data, Indian cleantech startups raised a record $433 Mn in Q3 2026, nearly 3X from $118 Mn in the year-ago quarter. Although funding remained heavily concentrated in one segment, the sector’s broader momentum was evident: deal count rose 44% YoY to 23, while average cheque size zoomed to $19 Mn from $7 Mn in Q3 2025.

The EV Concentration: Within cleantech, electric mobility dominated funding charts in Q3. Just three EV startups – River, Yulu and Ultraviolette – raised a combined $298 Mn, nearly 69% of the sector’s total haul in the quarter. The concentration highlights the sector’s over-dependence on a small group of well-funded ventures. 

Decoding The Boom: Cleantech funding surged as investors shifted their focus from climate narratives to commercially-viable businesses solving real problems. Electric mobility led the charge, supported by rising EV registrations, stronger consumer demand and improving PMF. What also helped was rising component localisation and growing investor confidence.

The Road Ahead: Experts believe that the sector’s long-term outlook will depend on broadening investment beyond EVs to other emerging areas such as energy storage, grid tech and green hydrogen. They also see deeper localisation improving margins and reducing supply chain risks. As such, unit economics and a clear path to sustainable revenues will be a key focus area for backers going forward. 

As investor conviction expanded across the cleantech ecosystem in Q3, why did capital remain tightly locked within a handful of EV players? Let’s find out…

From The Editor’s Desk

The AI Safety Drill

  • OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI giants are rehearsing how they would respond to a catastrophic incident involving AI. The companies are set to engage with US lawmakers as experts believe a major AI incident could happen within 12 months.
  • The planning comes as AI companies look to avoid a serious failure, which could prompt sweeping public backlash, new restrictions and scrutiny of industry leaders. The fear is that a major AI incident could impact internet infrastructure or financial systems.
  • The safety drill comes as LLMs find software vulnerabilities and coordinate agents. In the past few months, both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported several instances, where their agents bypassed safeguards and accessed real-world infrastructure.

Weekly Startup Funding Tanks

  • Indian startups managed to raise a cumulative $123 Mn last week, down 47% from $234 Mn in the preceding week. However, deal count more than doubled week-on-week to 25. DailyObjects and Lumio emerged as the most funded startups last week.
  • Ecommerce dominated the funding charts last week, raising $63.9 Mn across nine deals. Fintech ranked second with $24 Mn in funding, followed by advanced hardware and technology at $10 Mn. 
  • Early-stage funding trends remained strong as pre-seed and seed-stage startups collectively bagged $12.5 Mn across nine deals. 3one4 Capital and Fireside Ventures emerged as the most active investors, backing two startups each.

Mixed Week For Startup Stocks

  • Of the 66 new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s coverage, 36 gained in the range of 0.1% to nearly 25% last week. The remaining 30 fell in the range of 0.23% to 13.93%. MobiKwik and PW emerged as the biggest gainers, while Yudiz and Zappfresh shed the most.
  • The combined market capitalisation of 67 new-age tech stocks, including the recently listed AceVector, stood at $154.71 Bn at the end of last week compared to $153.61 Bn for 66 companies in the preceding week.
  • Going forward, investors will be tracking inflation data, crude oil prices, progress in Iran-US negotiations and global bond yields for market cues next week. 

Nat Habit Bags ₹142 Cr

  • The D2C personal care brand has raised around $14.7 Mn in its Series C round led by Trident Growth Partners to expand its distribution network, product portfolio and manufacturing capabilities.
  • Founded in 2019, Nat Habit sells Ayurveda-based personal care products, including hair oils, masks, scrubs, and face creams. Having served 60 Lakh customers so far, the D2C brand currently claims to clocking ₹330 Cr in annualised gross revenue.
  • The funding comes amid growing investor interest in the homegrown ayurvedic wellness segment, which is being driven by growing demand for traditional formulas, the rise of quick commerce, premiumisation and multi-functional products.

India’s Listed Startup Tracker

  • India is home to over 70 listed new-age tech companies, with a combined market capitalisation of $173 Bn. Of this, 18 startups went public in 2025 and another 15 have already crossed the milestone this year so far.
  • Together, these listed startups boast a combined revenue of $26 Bn. A majority of these new-age tech companies, nearly 74%, are profitable, while the remaining posted a cumulative loss of $932 Mn in FY26.
  • Delhi NCR is home to the largest number of listed startups. On the sectoral front, fintech and ecommerce account for the biggest chunk of listed new-age tech companies.

Inc42 Markets

Inc42 Startup Spotlight

Turning Agri-Waste Into Steel Industry’s Next Big Power Bet

India’s steel industry still runs largely on coal, while millions of tonnes of agricultural waste goes waste every year. Climitra is connecting these two problems by converting waste biomass into industrial-grade biochar, offering industries a route to carbon removal.

Turning Waste Into Fuel: Founded in 2025, Climitra is building a vertically-integrated startup to convert biomass into bio-coal. It uses AI and geospatial intelligence to map and assess biomass availability, and then converts locally-sourced waste into fuel through a proprietary pyrolysis process. 

A Coal Substitute: Climitra’s bio-coal is designed as a 1:1 replacement for fossil coal in steel-making, reducing the need for costly furnace retrofits. The startup claims that its output contains 75-85% fixed carbon, has a gross calorific value of 6,500–8,000 kcal/kg and can cut emissions by up to 90% compared with fossil coal.

Beyond Bio-Fuel: Climitra’s business model extends beyond bio-fuel. The startup is targeting both industrial decarbonisation and carbon removal, using its existing biomass supply chain. The startup claims it has already validated its bio-coal with Tata Steel, JSW Steel and AM/NS India. 

Backed by InfoEdge Ventures, the startup is eyeing a piece of the Indian biomass briquette market, which is projected to become a $2.1 Bn opportunity by 2032. So, can Climitra turn agricultural waste into a lower-carbon fuel for its steel industry?
